reference.source: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID) / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal recessive disorders of coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) biosynthesis caused by mutations in COQ genes (e.g. COQ2, COQ4, COQ8A/ADCK3, PDSS1/2), impairing electron transport between complexes I/II and III

It is one of the few treatable mitochondrial disorders: exogenous coenzyme Q10 supplementation can produce dramatic clinical benefit, especially when started early and before irreversible organ damage

Recognised clinical syndromes include a steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (notably with COQ2/COQ6), a severe infantile multisystem form, cerebellar ataxia (often COQ8A/ADCK3), and an encephalomyopathic form
Nephrotic syndrome due to CoQ10 deficiency is an important reversible cause and warrants a trial of supplementation rather than escalating immunosuppression alone

Muscle biopsy may show reduced activities of coenzyme Q10-dependent respiratory chain segments (complex I+III and II+III) with preserved complex-specific activities, and direct measurement of muscle coenzyme Q10 is diagnostically useful
Because the response to treatment can be striking, prompt recognition and a supplementation trial are central to management while awaiting genetic confirmation
reference.pathophysiology: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a lipid-soluble electron carrier that shuttles electrons from respiratory-chain complexes I and II to complex III and also serves as a lipophilic antioxidant. Biallelic mutations in genes of the coenzyme Q10 biosynthetic pathway reduce ubiquinone synthesis, impairing oxidative phosphorylation and increasing oxidative stress. Tissue involvement reflects the affected gene and residual synthesis, producing phenotypes ranging from isolated steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (podocyte-predominant) to cerebellar ataxia, encephalomyopathy, and severe multisystem infantile disease. Because the deficient metabolite can be partially replaced, exogenous supplementation may restore electron transport and reverse or arrest organ dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic or immune-mediated steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome
Hereditary cerebellar ataxias (e.g. ataxia with oculomotor apraxia, Friedreich ataxia)
Secondary coenzyme Q10 deficiency from other metabolic or mitochondrial disease
Leigh syndrome and other infantile mitochondrial encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Direct measurement of coenzyme Q10 in skeletal muscle (and cultured fibroblasts)
Respiratory-chain enzyme assays showing reduced combined complex I+III and II+III activities
Molecular genetic testing of COQ pathway genes (COQ2, COQ4, COQ6, COQ8A/ADCK3, PDSS1/2 and others)
Renal assessment including urinalysis and, where indicated, biopsy for podocyte involvement
Brain MRI and cerebellar imaging in ataxic/encephalopathic presentations
Plasma and CSF lactate as markers of mitochondrial dysfunction
redFlags: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome progressing towards renal failure that has not been trialled on coenzyme Q10
Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or multiorgan involvement in infancy
Emerging seizures or profound hypotonia indicating severe mitochondrial compromise
Progressive cerebellar ataxia with functional decline
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the genotype, affected organs, and how early treatment begins; some patients, particularly those with the nephrotic or ataxic forms, improve substantially with coenzyme Q10 supplementation, whereas severe infantile multisystem disease carries a poor prognosis despite treatment. Early supplementation before irreversible damage offers the best chance of benefit.
pitfalls: Escalating immunosuppression in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome without considering a treatable coenzyme Q10 deficiency
Delaying a supplementation trial while awaiting genetic results when clinical suspicion is high
Attributing the picture solely to a generic mitochondrial disorder and missing the specific, treatable defect
Failing to distinguish primary biosynthetic deficiency from secondary coenzyme Q10 reduction, which alters counselling and expectations
